name: Ahab
bio:
Ahab son of Omri succeeded his father as king of Israel, reigning twenty-two years in Samaria (1 Kings 16:28-29). Scripture introduces him with a damning verdict: he did more evil in the LORD's eyes than any king of Israel before him. As if walking in the sins of Jeroboam were a trivial thing, he married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and went on to serve and worship Baal, building a temple and altar for Baal in Samaria and making an Asherah pole — provoking the LORD to anger more than any king of Israel before him (1 Kings 16:30-33). In his reign, Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho, losing his firstborn son Abiram when he laid its foundations and his youngest son Segub when he set up its gates, in grim fulfillment of the curse Joshua had pronounced centuries earlier on anyone who rebuilt that city (1 Kings 16:34; compare Joshua 6:26). It was against this backdrop that the prophet Elijah confronted Ahab directly, announcing a drought that would last for years except at his word — a direct challenge to Baal, the storm god Ahab now served (1 Kings 17:1).

## 📖 Core Story: War with Ben-Hadad, and a Costly Mercy

Ben-Hadad, king of Syria, marched thirty-two allied kings against Samaria and besieged it, demanding Ahab's silver, gold, wives, and children — which Ahab conceded — then escalating to let Ben-Hadad's own men ransack every house in the city. Backed by the elders, Ahab refused this second demand, and Ben-Hadad vowed Samaria's dust wouldn't fill his army's hands; Ahab answered that one shouldn't boast of victory before the battle is even fought (1 Kings 20:1-12).

A prophet promised Ahab the LORD would deliver the vast army into his hand, and Israel's 232 young men routed the drunken Syrians, who fled with Ben-Hadad himself escaping on horseback (1 Kings 20:13-21). The next year Ben-Hadad returned at Aphek with a reorganized force, but Israel again crushed them — 100,000 Syrian footmen fell in a single day, and 27,000 more died when a wall collapsed on them. Ben-Hadad's servants, counting on Israel's kings being merciful, had him approach Ahab in sackcloth with a rope on his head; Ahab called him "my brother," set him in his own chariot, and let him go in exchange for restored cities and trade rights in Damascus (1 Kings 20:22-34). A disguised prophet then condemned Ahab for releasing a man the LORD had appointed to destruction, pronouncing that Ahab's own life and people would pay for Ben-Hadad's — and Ahab went home to Samaria heavy and displeased (1 Kings 20:35-43).

## 📖 Core Story: Naboth's Vineyard

When Naboth the Jezreelite refused to sell or trade his vineyard, which bordered Ahab's palace in Jezreel, Ahab sulked in bed and wouldn't eat. Jezebel had Naboth framed on false charges of cursing God and the king, and the men of his own city stoned him to death on her orders; she then told Ahab to go take possession of the vineyard, which he did (1 Kings 21:1-16). Elijah confronted Ahab in the vineyard itself with the LORD's judgment: dogs would lick Ahab's blood where they had licked Naboth's, his whole dynasty would be cut off like Jeroboam's and Baasha's, and dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel. Scripture adds that there was none like Ahab, who sold himself to wickedness, stirred up by Jezebel. Ahab tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and fasted in genuine humility, and for that the LORD delayed the disaster to his son's reign rather than his own (1 Kings 21:17-29).

## 📖 Core Story: Death at Ramoth Gilead

Three years of peace with Syria ended when Ahab resolved to retake Ramoth Gilead and persuaded Jehoshaphat of Judah to join him. Four hundred court prophets promised victory, but Ahab admitted he hated the one true prophet, Micaiah son of Imlah, because Micaiah never prophesied good for him. Summoned anyway, Micaiah foretold that Israel would scatter and Ahab would die, revealing that the LORD had sent a lying spirit into the mouths of the other prophets to lure Ahab to his death. Ahab had Micaiah imprisoned on bread and water and marched to battle regardless, disguising himself while Jehoshaphat wore royal robes (1 Kings 22:1-30).

A stray arrow struck Ahab between the joints of his armor; he was held upright in his chariot until he died at evening, his blood pooling in the chariot floor. When his chariot was later washed in the pool of Samaria, dogs licked up his blood, fulfilling the word Elijah had spoken over him at Naboth's vineyard. Ahab was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahaziah succeeded him (1 Kings 22:31-40).
